submission.method: Ran a Python 3.12 script with httpx 0.27 on an AWS EC2 t3.small in us-east-1, sending 500 sequential GET requests at 8 requests per second to /v2/search with 500 distinct US street addresses. Recorded wall-clock latency and status code per request; no retries.

Spot-checked 50 results against known coordinates: 47 were rooftop-level and 3 resolved only to the street centroid.

submission.use_case: Batch geocoding of delivery addresses for a routing prototype

subject.name: Node.js 22 built-in fetch behind an HTTP proxy

submission.summary: Node 22's global fetch ignored the HTTPS_PROXY environment variable and timed out behind a required proxy; installing undici's ProxyAgent with setGlobalDispatcher fixed it.
submission.method: In a container whose outbound traffic must go through an HTTP proxy, set HTTPS_PROXY and ran a script calling fetch('https://registry.npmjs.org/') on Node.js 22.11.0, 20 times. Then added undici 6.21.0, created a ProxyAgent from process.env.HTTPS_PROXY, installed it with setGlobalDispatcher before the first fetch, and ran 20 more times.

observations.observation: All 20 calls failed with UND_ERR_CONNECT_TIMEOUT after about 10 seconds, while curl in the same container honored HTTPS_PROXY and succeeded.
With setGlobalDispatcher(new ProxyAgent(process.env.HTTPS_PROXY)) at startup, all 20 calls succeeded with a median of 310 ms.
The dispatcher only applied to fetch; an older dependency using the https module still needed its own agent configuration.

submission.limitations: One network and proxy setup. Newer Node releases add opt-in environment proxy support, which this run did not test.

submission.summary: requests.get with no timeout hung for over 15 minutes against a server that accepted the connection but never answered; timeout=(3.05, 10) made it fail after 10 seconds.
submission.method: Started a local TCP server that accepts connections and never writes a response. Called requests.get against it 5 times with no timeout argument, killing each call after 15 minutes, then 5 times with timeout=(3.05, 10). Timed each call with time.perf_counter.

observations.observation: Without a timeout, none of the 5 calls returned; each was killed after 15 minutes.
With timeout=(3.05, 10), each run raised ReadTimeout after 10.0 to 10.1 seconds.
The library docs do say there is no default timeout; the behavior matches them but is easy to miss in a script.

submission.limitations: Simulated unresponsive server on localhost. Real network failures may show up as connection errors rather than hangs.

why: Inference throughput benchmark with hardware, flags, and plausible numbers for an 8B model on an L4.

submission.summary: On one NVIDIA L4, vLLM 0.6.3 serving Llama 3.1 8B in bf16 reached about 470 output tokens/s at 32 concurrent requests; median time to first token rose from 110 ms to 1.3 s.
submission.method: Launched vLLM's OpenAI-compatible server with --max-model-len 4096 and --gpu-memory-utilization 0.92 on a GCP g2-standard-8 instance. Used vLLM's benchmark_serving.py with 512-token prompts and 256 output tokens, 200 requests per run, at concurrency 1, 8 and 32. Reported medians over three runs per setting.

measurements.metric: median time to first token at 1
median time to first token at 32

observations.observation: Aggregate output throughput scaled almost linearly from 15.8 tok/s at 1 request to 470 tok/s at 32, since decoding stayed memory-bandwidth bound.
Median time to first token went from 110 ms to 1.3 s at concurrency 32 as prefills queued behind each other.
With max-model-len 4096 the server reported room for about 44,000 KV-cache tokens, enough that no requests were preempted at concurrency 32.

submission.limitations: Synthetic fixed-length prompts on one GPU type. Real traffic with mixed prompt lengths, or newer vLLM versions, will give different numbers.

subject.name: ripgrep search in a repository with gitignored build output

submission.summary: rg returned zero matches for a string that existed in the gitignored dist/ folder; adding --no-ignore found all 14 occurrences, the same as grep -rn but about 18 times faster.
submission.method: In a TypeScript monorepo with dist/ listed in .gitignore, searched for a known identifier with 'rg featureFlagX', then 'rg --no-ignore featureFlagX', then 'grep -rn featureFlagX .', and compared match counts and wall time with a warm disk cache.

observations.observation: ripgrep skipped dist/ because it respects .gitignore by default, and it reported no results rather than a notice about skipped paths.
rg --no-ignore returned the same 14 matches as grep and finished in 0.21 s against 3.8 s.
Files under .github/ were also skipped until adding --hidden, which is separate from --no-ignore.

submission.limitations: Documented behavior that is easy to miss in automation. One repository and filesystem; timings depend on cache state.

why: Query plan before and after an index change, with row counts and medians; explains the collation cause.

subject.name: PostgreSQL prefix LIKE queries on a btree index

submission.summary: A prefix LIKE search did a sequential scan despite a btree index because the database used en_US.UTF-8 collation; an index with text_pattern_ops cut the query from 820 ms to 3.1 ms.
submission.method: On a 4.2 million row products table, ran EXPLAIN ANALYZE for a query selecting id where sku LIKE 'AB12%' with a standard btree index on sku. Then created a second index on sku using text_pattern_ops and ran the same query 10 times after one warm-up run.

observations.observation: With only the default btree index, the plan was a parallel sequential scan, because an index built with a non-C collation cannot serve LIKE prefix matches.
After adding the text_pattern_ops index, the planner used an index scan and median time dropped to 3.1 ms.
The extra index added 160 MB and only helps pattern queries; equality lookups and sorting on sku still used the original index.

submission.limitations: One table and one collation. Databases created with C collation, ILIKE, or leading wildcards behave differently.

submission.summary: stripe.webhooks.constructEvent rejected each test event because express.json() had already parsed the body; switching the webhook route to express.raw made all 25 events verify.
submission.method: Sent 25 test events with the Stripe CLI (stripe listen --forward-to localhost:3000/webhook) to an Express handler that calls constructEvent with the endpoint's signing secret. First with app.use(express.json()) applied globally, then with express.raw({ type: 'application/json' }) on the webhook route only.

observations.observation: With the JSON body parser in front, constructEvent got a parsed object instead of the original bytes and failed with 'No signatures found matching the expected signature for payload'.
express.raw on the /webhook route alone made all 25 events verify, while other routes kept JSON parsing.
The error did not mention body parsing, which made the cause slow to find.

submission.limitations: Test-mode events and one framework only. Other frameworks need their own way to reach the raw request body.
